title: What m does to a line

files.lesson.md: --- order: 6 unit: lines node: AC9M8A04 n1 uses: [AC9M7A05 n3, AC9M7N07 n2] # plotting a line from its rule; negative m gives negative outputs assumes: [AC9M8A02] # its Prior Knowledge; only graphing a line from a rule is used, taught in Plotting a rule (7A05 n3). Equations with x on both sides and inequalities are class work title: What m does to a line summary: In y = mx + c, the number in front of x sets how steep the line is and which way it goes. language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Ramps, roofs, ski runs and phone bills all have a steepness: how much more for each step along. In a rule like y = 3x + 1, one number decides it." connection: road-gradient # data/connections/maths.yml app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8135 url: http://127.0.0.1:8135/index.html readySelector: "#sl-m" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: graph.yml#explain-pic, caption: "$y = 3x + 1$: one step right, up 3. That 3 is $m$." } explainClip: query: { code: "@graph.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "m is how far the line goes up for each step right" say: "m is how far the line goes up for each step to the right." clip: - caption: { text: "Here m = 1: one step right, up 1.", say: "Here m is one: one step right, and up one." } - wait: 400 - caption: { text: "A bigger m: up 2 for each step, so the line is steeper.", say: "Make m bigger: up two for each step, so the line is steeper." } - click: Make m bigger - wait: 400 - caption: { text: "m = 3: up 3. The line still crosses the y-axis at 1.", say: "m is three: up three, and it still crosses the y axis at one." } - click: Make m bigger - wait: 400 - caption: { text: "m = 0: no steps up, so the line is flat.", say: "When m is zero, there are no steps up, so the line is flat." } - click: Make m smaller - click: Make m smaller - click: Make m smaller - wait: 400 - caption: { text: "A negative m goes down: m = −2 is down 2 for each step right.", say: "A negative m goes down: m of negative two is down two each step." } - click: Make m smaller - click: Make m smaller - expect: { selector: "#legend", contains: "y = −2x + 1" } - wait: 1200 --- A rule such as $y = 3x + 1$ gives a **straight line**: work out $y$ for each value of $x$, plot the points, and join them. Every rule of the form $y = mx + c$ gives a straight line. $m$ is the number in front of $x$, and $c$ is the number on its own. Keep $c$ at 1 for now, and watch what $m$ does. ## Predict: a bigger m ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to how the line will change before touching the slider makes the board a test of their idea about m, not a demonstration." check: type: predict q: "The line $y = x + 1$ has $m = 1$. If $m$ becomes 3, so the rule is $y = 3x + 1$, what happens to the line?" options: - "It gets steeper, and still crosses the $y$-axis at 1" - "It moves up by 2, and is just as steep" - "It gets less steep" - "It moves 2 to the right" actual: "It gets steeper. When x = 0, y is still 1 (3 × 0 + 1 = 1), so the line still crosses the y-axis at 1, but now y goes up 3 for each step right instead of 1." ``` $$y = x + 1 \quad\longrightarrow\quad y = 3x + 1$$ Think about two points on each line: where $x = 0$, and where $x = 1$. Which one moves? ## Run: change m ```step stage: run insight: "Moving m while c stays fixed shows the line turning about the point (0, 1): m changes the steepness, not where the line crosses the y-axis." try: { playground: board, starter: "graph.yml#run", height: 640 } check: { type: board, text: "Set $m$ to 3. Was your prediction right?", when: "m = 3" } ``` Change $m$ with the slider, or the − and + buttons. Watch three things: the line, the table, and the orange step, which shows how far the line goes up for one step to the right. ## Investigate: reading m ```step stage: investigate insight: "m is how far y goes up for each step of 1 to the right. The table and the step both show it, and it is the same all along the line." tasks: - picture: { ref: graph.yml#explain-pic, caption: "$y = 3x + 1$: from $x = 1$ to $x = 2$, $y$ goes from 4 to 7: up 3." } check: type: answer q: "In $y = 5x + 1$, how far does the line go up for each step of 1 to the right?" answer: "5" feedback: - ["1", "1 is c, the number on its own: it is where the line crosses the y-axis. Look at the number in front of x."] - ["6", "6 is the value of y when x = 1. How much did y go up from x = 0 to x = 1?"] explain: "5. Each step right adds one more lot of 5 to 5x, so y goes up by 5 each time." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#lee" text: "Lee decides which line is steeper. Click the line where his reasoning goes wrong." answer: 4 fault: logic misconception: m-c-swap explain: "Line 4: 4 and 1 are where the lines cross the y-axis, not how steep they are. Steepness is the number in front of x: 3 is more than 2, so y = 3x + 1 is steeper." - check: type: answer q: "On the line $y = 3x + 1$, how far does $y$ go up from $x = 5$ to $x = 6$?" answer: "3" feedback: - ["16", "16 is the value of y when x = 5. Work out y at x = 6 too, then find the difference."] - ["19", "19 is the value of y when x = 6. How much bigger is it than y at x = 5?"] explain: "At x = 5, y = 16; at x = 6, y = 19. Up 3, the same as from x = 0 to x = 1: m is the same all along the line." ``` ### Up for each step right Here is how to read $m$ from a rule, by working out $y$ one step at a time. ```worked y = 3x + 1 :: How far does this line go up for each step right? Start with the rule. x = 0: \; y = 3(0) + 1 = 1 :: Work out $y$ where $x$ is 0. x = 1: \; y = 3(1) + 1 = 4 :: One step right: $x$ goes from 0 to 1. 4 - 1 = 3 :: $y$ went up by 3. x = 2: \; y = 3(2) + 1 = 7, \; 7 - 4 = 3 :: Another step right: up 3 again. m = 3 :: Each step right adds one more lot of 3, so $y$ goes up by $m$, the number in front of $x$. ``` ### Find the mistake Read Lee's working one line at a time. Which line compares the wrong thing? ### Further along Does the line go up by the same amount everywhere, or only near the start? ## Modify: change m on purpose ```step stage: modify insight: "Changing one thing at a time shows the whole rule: a bigger m is steeper, m = 0 is flat, a negative m goes down, and m need not be a whole number." try: { playground: board, starter: "graph.yml#through-9", height: 560 } tasks: - starter: "graph.yml#through-9" hint: ["The line starts at (0, 1). How far up is 9 from 1?", "That rise happens over 2 steps right. How far up for each step?"] check: { type: board, text: "Set $m$ so the line passes through $T(2, 9)$.", when: "T on y = mx + 1", explain: "m = 4: from (0, 1), up 4 and up 4 again reaches (2, 9)." } - starter: "graph.yml#flat" hint: "T is at the same height as where the line starts. How far up for each step right?" check: { type: board, text: "Set $m$ so the line passes through $T(3, 1)$.", when: "T on y = mx + 1", explain: "m = 0: y = 0x + 1 = 1 for every x, so the line is flat." } - starter: "graph.yml#down" hint: ["T is below where the line starts. Which way must the line go?", "From 1 down to −3 is down 4, over 2 steps right."] check: { type: board, text: "Set $m$ so the line passes through $T(2, -3)$.", when: "T on y = mx + 1", explain: "m = −2: y goes down 2 for each step right. A negative m makes the line go down." } - starter: "graph.yml#half" hint: "From (0, 1) to T is up 2 over 4 steps right. How far up for one step?" check: { type: board, text: "Set $m$ so the line passes through $T(4, 3)$.", when: "T on y = mx + 1", explain: "m = 0.5: up half a square for each step right, so up 2 over 4 steps." } ``` ### Steeper Each task puts a point $T$ on the board. Find the $m$ that takes the line through $T(2, 9)$. Change only $m$. ### Flat Now take the line through $T(3, 1)$. What does the line do? ### Down $T(2, -3)$ is below the start of the line. Which way must it go? ### Less than 1 Take the line through $T(4, 3)$. The slider now moves in halves. ## Practise: read the line ```step stage: practise insight: "Reading m from a rule, from a description and from a point are the same skill; the review question keeps substitution from the Equations unit fresh." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "What is $m$ in $y = 4x - 2$?" answer: "4" feedback: - ["-2", "−2 is c, the number on its own: it is where the line crosses the y-axis. m is the number in front of x."] explain: "m = 4: the line goes up 4 for each step right." - check: type: question q: "Which line goes down from left to right?" options: ["$y = 3x - 2$", "$y = -2x + 5$", "$y = 0x + 4$"] answer: 1 explain: "Only a negative m makes a line go down: y = −2x + 5 goes down 2 for each step right. The −2 in y = 3x − 2 is c, so that line still goes up 3 for each step; y = 0x + 4 is flat." - check: type: answer q: "The line $y = mx + 1$ passes through $(3, 7)$. What is $m$?" answer: "2" feedback: - ["7", "7 is y at x = 3. The line starts at 1 when x = 0: how far does it go up over the 3 steps?"] - ["6", "6 is how far it goes up over 3 steps. How far for each step?"] explain: "From (0, 1) to (3, 7) is up 6 over 3 steps right, so up 2 for each step: m = 2." smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "The line starts at $(0, 1)$ and reaches $(3, 7)$. How far does it go up altogether?", answer: 6, explain: "From 1 up to 7 is 6. That's over 3 steps right." } - check: type: answer q: "Review: work out $y$ when $x = 4$ in $y = 3x - 5$." answer: "7" feedback: - ["29", "It looks like 3x became 34. 3x means 3 × x, so it is 3 × 4 = 12."] - ["12", "That is 3 × 4. Now take away 5."] explain: "3 × 4 − 5 = 12 − 5 = 7." ``` ### From the rule ### Which way? ### From a point ### Review ## Make: your own line ```step stage: make insight: "Choosing m first and then finding a point on that line reverses the lesson: from the number to the picture." try: { playground: board, starter: "graph.yml#make", height: 560 } hint: ["Pick a value of m first, say m = 2.", "Start at (0, 1) and count: 1 right, 2 up. Drag P to that point, or count further along."] check: { type: board, text: "Choose any $m$, then drag $P$ onto your line, to the right of the $y$-axis.", when: "P on y = mx + 1 and x(P) > 0", explain: "P is on your line: its coordinates make y = mx + 1 true." } ``` Choose your own steepness with the slider. Then use counting (1 right, $m$ up) to find a point on your line and drag $P$ there. Try a negative $m$ too. Stretch: without the board, give a point on $y = 3x + 1$ where $x = 10$. ## Make: how steep is the hill, on paper ```step stage: make insight: "A road sign's percentage is m written as up per 100 along: rise divided by run, and a bigger m is steeper." hint: ["How far up for each 1 m along? Divide the rise by the run.", "A percentage is the climb in every 100 m along, so multiply the answer by 100."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "Hill A climbs 6 m while you travel 75 m along the flat. A sign on Hill B says 10%. On paper, work out Hill A's gradient as a percentage, then say which hill is steeper." steps: - ["$m = \\text{rise} \\div \\text{run} = 6 \\div 75$", "m is how far up for each step along"] - ["$6 \\div 75 = 0.08$, up 0.08 m for each metre along, so 8 m up in 100 m: 8%", "a percentage is the climb in 100 m along"] - ["Hill B is 10%, which is bigger than 8%, so Hill B is steeper", "a bigger m is a steeper line"] picks: - step: 1 q: "How do you find m from a climb of 6 m over 75 m along?" options: - "Divide the rise by the run: 6 ÷ 75" - "Divide the run by the rise: 75 ÷ 6" - "Take the rise from the run: 75 − 6" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "75 ÷ 6 is how far along for each metre up, the upside-down of m.", "Gradient compares the two distances. Subtracting does not say how steep it is."] answer: "8" tolerance: 0 feedback: - ["0.08", "That is the gradient as a decimal. A sign shows a percentage: how far up in 100 m along."] - ["12.5", "That is 75 ÷ 6, upside down. Divide the rise by the run."] criteria: - "I divided the rise by the run." - "I changed the decimal into a percentage by finding the climb in 100 m." - "I compared 8% and 10% and said which is steeper." explain: "6 ÷ 75 = 0.08, which is 8 m up in every 100 m: 8%. Hill B at 10% is steeper." ``` Do this one in your book, not on the screen. The hill is made up for the task, and a real sign gives the steepest part of the road. Divide, change it to a percentage, and compare. **Also used in** - **Roads and ramps.** A sign of 8% says the same thing as a line with $m = 0.08$. - **Roofs.** A roof pitch is the rise for each step along, so a steeper roof has a bigger $m$. - **Skiing and cycling.** Runs and hill climbs are rated by how much they go up for each distance along. ```teacher summary: Students vary m in y = mx + 1 on a graph board and find that m is how far the line goes up for each step right (AC9M8A04, node 1). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 15 min · Modify 12 min · Practise and Make 10 min goals: - I can describe what happens to the line y = mx + c when m gets bigger, is 0, or is negative. - I can read m from a rule as how far the line goes up for each step right. - I can find m for a line through (0, 1) and another point. struggle: "Believing a bigger number lifts the line instead of tilting it. Ask: where does the line cross the y-axis, before and after?" before: > Do the Run and Modify boards yourself first. Students should already be able to plot a line from a rule or a table, and work with negative numbers. Only m changes in this lesson: c stays at 1, so every line passes through (0, 1). What c does, and parallel lines, is the next lesson. If students ask about c, say "hold that thought": separating the two is the point. The lesson says "up for each step right" rather than "rise over run" or "gradient". The primer has the formal words if you want to introduce them at the end. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands for each option. The common wrong answer is 'moves up by 2': students expect a bigger number to lift the line. Do not correct it yet." - "Run: ask students to watch the point where the line crosses the y-axis as they move m. It never moves. Then point at the orange step and the table: both show the same number as m." - "Investigate: model the worked example live. Write y = 3x + 1, then work out y at x = 0, 1 and 2 at writing pace, saying 'one step right, how far up?' each time. Reveal the prepared lines afterwards to compare." - "Modify: each task changes one thing. Before the flat and down tasks, ask: what m do you think it will be? Then let them check." - "Practise: the 'which way' question plants a minus sign in c. Ask a student who chose y = 3x − 2 to work out y at x = 0 and x = 1." - "Make: collect a few students' m and P. Check one as a class: start at (0, 1), count 1 right, m up." - "Paper: the hill task in Make is worked in books; the page marks the percentage (8) and the reason for rise divided by run. Books out, then compare each step with the model." stuck: - see: A student says a bigger m moves the line up. ask: Where does the line cross the y-axis when m is 1? When m is 3? fix: "Work out y at x = 0 for both rules: 1 × 0 + 1 and 3 × 0 + 1 are both 1. The crossing point stays; only the steepness changes." - see: A student reads c as the steepness (Lee's mistake). ask: Which number changes how much y goes up each time x goes up by 1? fix: Make a two-row table for x = 0 and x = 1 and find the difference in y. It is the number in front of x. - see: A student cannot find m for the down task. ask: Is T above or below where the line starts? Which way must the line go? fix: "Count from (0, 1) to T: how far down, over how many steps right? Down means a negative m." - see: A student moves the slider until it works without noticing why. ask: Before you move it, what value of m do you think you need, and why? fix: Have them say the count aloud first ('2 steps right, up 8, so 4 each step'), then set the slider. stretch: "Find m for a line through (0, 1) and (6, 4). Then: which is steeper, y = −3x + 1 or y = 2x + 1? (Steepness is the size of m; the sign gives the direction.)" support: "Use the Run board for the Investigate questions: set m to the number in the rule and read the table. Give squared paper to count steps by hand." leads: > Next: what c does (the line moves up and down without turning) and parallel lines (same m). Then solving equations with graphs, where 2x + 3 = 11 becomes the point where y = 2x + 3 meets y = 11, and modelling with two lines. Where it leads in class: any rate. Dollars per hour, kilometres per hour, litres per minute: the steepness of the graph is the rate, and m in the rule is the same number. exit: q: "Without plotting, describe the line y = −2x + 1: where does it cross the y-axis, which way does it go, and how steep is it?" a: It crosses the y-axis at 1 and goes down 2 for each step to the right (m = −2). explain: > In a rule like $y = 3x + 1$, the number in front of $x$ is called $m$. It tells you how far the line goes **up for each step of 1 to the right**. Work it out one step at a time: when $x = 0$, $y = 1$; when $x = 1$, $y = 4$; when $x = 2$, $y = 7$. Each step right, $y$ goes up by 3. That is $m$. A bigger $m$ makes the line steeper. $m = 0$ makes it flat. A negative $m$ makes it go down. Changing $m$ does not move where the line crosses the $y$-axis: that is the number on its own, $c$. ```

# Graph boards for "What m does to a line". The rule is always y = mx + 1: c stays at 1 so that only m changes.

# region: run
widget: graph
x: -1, 5
y: -4, 16
slider m: 0, 4, 1
plot: y = mx + 1
table: 0, 1, 2, 3
step: 1
# endregion

# region: through-9
widget: graph
x: -1, 5
y: -4, 14
slider m: -4, 4, 1
plot: y = mx + 1
point T: 2, 9
step: 0
# endregion

# region: flat
widget: graph
x: -1, 5
y: -4, 14
slider m: -4, 4, 2
plot: y = mx + 1
point T: 3, 1
step: 0
# endregion

# region: down
widget: graph
x: -1, 5
y: -8, 8
slider m: -4, 4, 1
plot: y = mx + 1
point T: 2, -3
step: 0
# endregion

# region: half
widget: graph
x: -1, 5
y: -4, 8
slider m: -2, 2, 1, 0.5
plot: y = mx + 1
point T: 4, 3
step: 0
# endregion

# region: make
widget: graph
x: -1, 6
y: -6, 12
slider m: -3, 3, 1
plot: y = mx + 1
point P: 4, -4, drag
# endregion

# region: explain
widget: graph
x: -1, 4
y: -6, 12
slider m: -3, 3, 1
plot: y = mx + 1
step: 1
# endregion

# region: explain-pic
widget: graph
x: -1, 4
y: -2, 14
plot: y = 3x + 1
point A: 1, 4
point B: 2, 7
step: 1
# endregion
